questions.stem: An insurer's claims-notes assistant calls the Claude API with a fixed system prompt and retrieval over policy documents. Adjusters correct its drafts several times a day. The head of claims tells the steering group that, "like a new hire", the assistant will get better on its own as adjusters keep correcting it, so no engineering budget is needed next quarter. Which response BEST aligns the sponsor's expectations with how the system actually improves?

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt instructing Claude to remember adjusters' corrections from earlier chats and apply them when drafting future notes, then confirm to the sponsor that it now learns from use.

Append the complete, growing log of adjuster corrections to the system prompt of every request, so the model has seen every past correction before it drafts, and report the log's size to the group monthly.

Explain that the model does not update itself from usage (each request is stateless), then propose the loop that does improve it: capture corrections, make recurring ones eval cases, fix prompt or retrieval, and measure.
Tell the sponsor the assistant will be retrained on the insurer's corrections with each new model release, so accuracy will rise automatically over time without a dedicated budget or any new process.

questions.explanation: A hosted Claude model does not learn from an organization's traffic. The Messages API is stateless: every request carries only the context you send, and nothing an adjuster corrected yesterday changes how the model behaves today. Improvement therefore has to be engineered. Capture the corrections, triage them into eval cases, change what you control (prompt, examples, retrieval), confirm the gain on the eval set and report it. Saying this plainly, with the budget the loop needs, is the expectation-alignment job; letting the "new hire" story stand guarantees disappointment next quarter.

whyWrong.A: An instruction can't reach conversations the model never sees. Each request starts from the context you send, so 'remember earlier corrections' has nothing to act on, and the sponsor is left believing a false story.
whyWrong.B: An ever-growing, unreviewed log bloats every request, adds cost and noise, and nobody measures whether it helps. Curated examples selected through evals are the disciplined version of this idea.
whyWrong.D: New model releases are not tailored to this insurer's corrections, and the team has no lever to make them so. It promises something the architecture cannot deliver and removes the budget that real improvement needs.

questions.mindset: Models don't learn from your traffic; improvement is a loop you design, fund and measure.

questions.stem: A CFO has read that the model behind a new invoice-coding assistant "scores over 90% on a leading reasoning benchmark" and tells the steering group the assistant should therefore be "at least 90% accurate from day one". The team's eval on 500 real invoices from the last quarter currently shows 81% correct general-ledger codes. Which response BEST aligns the CFO's expectations?

options.text: Explain that benchmarks measure general tasks, not this task on this data; present the 81% from the representative eval with its failure categories and fix plan, and agree targets and checkpoints on that eval.

Switch to the model with the highest published benchmark score and tell the CFO that 90% will follow at launch, since stronger general reasoning transfers directly to coding invoices against the chart of accounts.

Re-run the eval on the subset of clean, machine-readable invoices, where accuracy is already above 90%, and report that figure to the steering group so the launch number matches what the CFO has read.

Accept the 90% target in the SLA now, on the grounds that 500 invoices is too small a sample to contradict a published benchmark, and plan to revisit the number once a full quarter of production data exists.

questions.explanation: A published benchmark says how a model performs on the benchmark's tasks. The only number that predicts this assistant's accuracy is an eval built to mirror its real work, which is exactly what the 500 real invoices are. Anthropic's guidance on choosing a model says to create benchmark tests specific to your use case and to test with your actual prompts and data. The architect's job is to make that measured result the shared reference point, explain where the gap comes from, and agree a target, plan and checkpoints against it rather than against a headline from an article.

whyWrong.B: Model choice is one lever among many, and a general benchmark does not predict performance on this task. Promising 90% before measuring is a guess dressed up as a plan.
whyWrong.C: Grading only the easy invoices manufactures a number. Expectations set on it will collapse the first week messy or scanned invoices arrive in production.
whyWrong.D: Five hundred real invoices are far better evidence than a benchmark on unrelated tasks. Signing up to 90% now writes an untested promise into the contract.

questions.mindset: Benchmarks describe benchmarks; your own representative eval describes your system.

questions.stem: A utility company wants to promise 99.99% availability for an outage-reporting assistant that calls the Claude API. In a load test, a small share of requests failed with transient server-side errors such as 529 overloaded and 500 api_error, and succeeded on retry. The operations director asks what the architect can responsibly commit to. Which response is BEST?

options.text: Commit to 99.99% for the whole assistant, since the failures seen in the load test were transient and the SDK retries them automatically with exponential backoff, so customers will rarely notice any degradation in practice.

Decline any availability commitment, explaining that because the assistant depends on an external model provider's API, its uptime is outside the team's control entirely and should not be promised to customers in writing.

Switch to the largest available model, since higher-capability models are served with more provider-side headroom and are more robust under load, and commit to 99.99% once a second load test passes cleanly.

Define availability for the whole service, counting successful retries with backoff and a degraded mode (queue the report, fallback form, route to staff), and name the provider dependency explicitly in the SLA.

questions.explanation: The business needs outage reports captured even when the model is briefly unavailable. The architecture can promise that by treating the model call as a dependency with retries and exponential backoff for transient errors, plus a degraded path that still accepts and queues the report or hands it to staff. The SLA then describes what the service guarantees (the report is never lost, and is answered within a stated time) and is honest that full AI answers depend on an external API. Anthropic's errors page documents 529 and 500 as transient conditions where retrying with backoff is appropriate.

whyWrong.A: Automatic retries with backoff reduce failures but can't guarantee four nines for a dependency you don't control. Committing to 99.99% without a degraded mode is over-promising.
whyWrong.B: Refusing to commit ignores what the team does control: retries, queueing and fallbacks. Stakeholders still need a usable promise.
whyWrong.C: Model size has nothing to do with API availability, and provider-side headroom for larger models does not remove the dependency risk. This changes cost and latency without addressing it.

questions.mindset: Promise what the whole service can guarantee, with graceful degradation around external dependencies.

questions.stem: A travel company's booking assistant runs comfortably today. Marketing has just told the architect that a TV campaign next month is expected to multiply peak traffic roughly tenfold for a weekend, and the CMO wants confirmation that "the AI will keep up." Nobody has checked the API account's limits. What should the architect do FIRST to give a reliable answer?

options.text: Confirm that it will keep up, because API rate limits are raised automatically as an organization's usage grows, and set up an error alert so the team can react if failures start appearing during the campaign weekend.

Compare projected peak requests and input/output tokens per minute against the organization's per-model rate limits, request any higher limits in advance, and agree the degraded behavior to show if limits are still hit.

Move all booking conversations to the Message Batches API for the campaign weekend, because batch processing has separate rate limits and is billed at a discount, so the live traffic spike is absorbed at lower cost.

Ask marketing to delay the campaign until the team can rebuild the assistant as a multi-agent system that spreads the load across several specialized agents, each carrying its own share of the traffic.

questions.explanation: Capacity is part of expectation alignment. Claude API rate limits are set per organization and per model, measured as requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, and exceeding them returns 429 errors. The responsible answer is to size the peak against those limits, request an increase in advance (the docs also warn that sharp usage spikes can trigger acceleration limits, so ramping traffic matters), and agree with the CMO what users see if limits are still hit. Prompt caching can also stretch input-token headroom, since cache reads don't count toward ITPM for most models.

whyWrong.A: Limits are tied to usage tier and do not rise to meet a sudden spike; sharp increases can even trigger acceleration limits. Promising capacity and hoping alerts fire in time is how campaigns fail publicly.
whyWrong.C: Batches are asynchronous with no completion-time guarantee, so they cannot serve a customer waiting in a live booking chat, whatever their separate limits or discount.
whyWrong.D: Splitting work across agents doesn't create API capacity and usually uses more tokens. It delays the business for no capacity gain.

questions.mindset: Check capacity limits against projected demand before promising scale; plan the degraded path.

questions.stem: A claims-triage assistant is used by four business units. Each unit lead emails the architect separately with different questions ("is it getting better?", "why did cost jump?", "when will the fraud flags be fixed?"), and the answers given to each lead have started to conflict. The architect wants to set up a monthly stakeholder review that keeps expectations aligned. Which TWO elements will MOST improve alignment? Choose TWO.

options.text: A live demo at each review of the newest features on a set of hand-picked example claims, so leads can see the improvements for themselves and build enthusiasm for the roadmap.
The same small dashboard every month: quality against the agreed eval target, latency against the SLA, cost per claim, and the top failure categories with trend lines.
A separate tailored report for each unit lead, written to highlight the metrics that unit cares about most, so every lead feels their priorities are being addressed.
A shared decision and issue log listing open problems, the options and trade-offs, the owner who decides on each, and what has changed since the last review because of feedback.
A quarterly rather than monthly cadence, so there is enough time between reviews for the engineering team to ship meaningful changes without the distraction of preparing updates.

questions.explanation: Conflicting answers come from having no single, shared source of truth. A fixed dashboard shown to everyone, every time (quality versus target, latency versus SLA, cost per task, top failure categories), lets all units see the same numbers and trends. A shared decision and issue log makes trade-offs explicit, names who decides, and shows what changed as a result of feedback, which closes the loop. Together they turn scattered email threads into one regular feedback cycle anchored in eval results.

whyWrong.A: Hand-picked demos show the best case, not the measured performance. They inflate expectations instead of aligning them.
whyWrong.C: Tailored reports per lead are what caused the conflicting stories. Everyone needs the same numbers, even if they focus on different rows.
whyWrong.E: Making reviews less frequent lengthens the feedback loop and leaves more time for expectations to drift between units.

questions.mindset: One shared, recurring view of metrics and decisions beats many private conversations.

questions.stem: A software vendor's product-question assistant serves both its sales team and its support team. Sales asks for longer, more persuasive answers that mention add-on products. Support asks for shorter answers that solve the problem and never upsell. Over three weeks, engineers have changed the system prompt back and forth four times as each group complains, and both groups now say quality is "unstable." What should the architect do?

options.text: Pick the length and tone that splits the difference between the two requests, write it into the system prompt, and tell both groups that a compromise is the fairest outcome for the product.
Let the model decide the style for each answer by adding an instruction to infer from the message whether the asker is from sales or support, and to adapt length and tone accordingly.
Bring both leads together with examples, agree per-audience success criteria with the business owner, then give each audience its own prompt configuration measured against its own rubric.
Freeze the prompt and stop accepting style requests until the end of the quarter, since the constant changes are what is making quality feel unstable for everyone who uses the assistant.

questions.explanation: The two groups have genuinely different needs, so prompt ping-pong can never satisfy both. The architect should surface the conflict explicitly, get the business owner to agree success criteria for each audience, and then encode that in the design: the caller is known, so each audience can get its own prompt or configuration, measured against its own rubric. Changes then stop undoing each other, and each group can see improvement on its own criteria. Anthropic's eval guidance calls for specific, measurable criteria tied to the use case.

whyWrong.A: A compromise that neither group asked for leaves both unhappy and still hides the real disagreement from the business owner.
whyWrong.B: Asking the model to infer the audience from the message adds an unreliable step when the application already knows who is calling. It also leaves the success criteria undefined.
whyWrong.D: Freezing changes ignores real feedback and damages trust. The problem is missing criteria, not the number of changes.

questions.mindset: When stakeholder feedback conflicts, make the conflict explicit, agree criteria per audience, and design for it.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, the number of issue reports from users of an internal IT-helpdesk assistant has dropped sharply. In interviews, staff say they stopped reporting problems because "nothing ever seems to happen." The team has in fact fixed many reported problems, but quietly. What is the MOST effective way to restore the feedback loop?

options.text: Close the loop visibly: acknowledge every report, show its current status, and publish short release notes that link each fix back to the report that prompted it.
Offer a small prize each month to the employee who submits the most issue reports, so that reporting volume returns quickly to its earlier level and staff feel the channel matters.
Treat the drop in reports as a sign that quality has improved, and reallocate the team's triage time toward building new features that staff have asked for.
Have the assistant ask at the end of every conversation whether the user ran into any problems, so feedback is collected in the flow of work without relying on separate reports.

questions.explanation: People keep giving feedback when they can see it acted on. Acknowledging reports, showing their status and announcing what changed because of them tells staff their effort matters, which restores the signal. It also helps stakeholders calibrate their expectations, because they see which issues are fixed and which are still open. Closing the loop with the people who reported issues is what keeps an eval-driven, continuous iteration process supplied with real failure cases.

whyWrong.B: Paying for volume rewards quantity over quality and attracts low-value reports; volume going back up is not evidence the loop works. It doesn't fix the reason people stopped reporting.
whyWrong.C: The interviews show the drop comes from lost trust, not better quality. Treating silence as success hides real problems.
whyWrong.D: Asking at the end of every chat adds friction and still doesn't show people that their feedback leads to anything.

questions.mindset: Feedback loops only stay alive when people can see their input acted on.

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain's medication-question assistant has a quality SLA of "at least 95% of answers rated acceptable on the monthly eval sample." It has met that target every month. However, last month two answers gave a wrong dosage interval, and the clinical lead says the SLA is "measuring the wrong thing." Which TWO changes to the SLA and its supporting design are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add a separate commitment for critical errors such as dosage facts, with a near-zero target, backed by a deterministic check against the drug database or a pharmacist review gate.
Raise the headline acceptance target from 95% to 99%, since a higher overall accuracy bar will naturally squeeze out the dangerous mistakes along with the minor ones.
Add an instruction telling the assistant to double-check every dosage before answering, and report the share of answers where it confirmed its own dosage as a new SLA metric.
Remove dosage questions from the monthly eval sample, because they are a small share of traffic and including them makes the overall acceptance rate harder for the board to interpret.
Grade and report errors by severity category using a rubric agreed with the clinical lead, so a harmless phrasing slip and a wrong dose are never counted the same.

questions.explanation: A single acceptance rate treats a clumsy sentence and a dangerous dose as equal. The SLA should report errors by severity, with a rubric agreed by the clinical owner, and set a separate, much stricter target for critical errors. Because a prompt cannot guarantee that target, the design must back it with a deterministic control (checking dosage against an authoritative source) or a human review gate. Anthropic's success-criteria guidance models exactly this: multidimensional criteria that separate errors causing inconvenience from egregious ones, rather than one headline rate.

whyWrong.B: A higher overall rate can still be met while dangerous errors continue. It doesn't change what is measured, only the threshold.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking is a prompt-only fix, and the model confirming its own answer is not independent evidence that the dose is right.
whyWrong.D: Removing the riskiest questions from the eval hides exactly the failures that matter most. That games the metric.

questions.mindset: Weight quality by severity, and back critical commitments with deterministic or human controls.

questions.stem: A bank's document-extraction service missed its quarterly straight-through-processing SLA (88% against a 93% commitment). Analysis shows the overall drop is driven almost entirely by a new mortgage-application form introduced in the second month, which the eval set doesn't cover. The quarterly business review is tomorrow. What should the architect present?

options.text: Report the overall figure as 'on track' by excluding the new mortgage form from the calculation, since it was not part of the scope when the SLA was originally agreed with the business.
Announce that the team will move to the most capable model next week, which should recover the gap on the new form, and commit to 93% next quarter without changing anything else in the pipeline.
Present the headline miss without the breakdown, apologize, and promise the team will work harder next quarter, keeping the technical detail out of the business conversation.
Show the miss openly with the form-type breakdown, explain the cause, and offer costed options (add the form to evals and fix, route it to human review, or adjust scope) for the owner to choose.

questions.explanation: When reality diverges from the commitment, the architect should show the data, explain the root cause and give the business owner real choices with their costs, then record the decision. Here the cause is clear and specific: a new input type outside the eval set. Options such as adding that form to the evals and fixing it, routing it to human review in the meantime, or agreeing a separate target for it let the owner decide with full information. Adding the new form to the eval set is also how the gap is prevented from reappearing.

whyWrong.A: Quietly redefining the scope after a miss destroys trust. Any scope change must be agreed openly, not applied to make a number look better.
whyWrong.B: Promising a model swap fixes before diagnosis is a guess. The cause is an untested input type, and nothing has been evaluated yet.
whyWrong.C: Hiding the breakdown leaves the business unable to choose, and 'work harder' is not a plan. The cause is known and should be shared.

questions.mindset: Report misses transparently with root cause and costed options; let the owner decide.

questions.stem: An architect's implementation guide includes a nine-step procedure for adding a new tool to the team's agent: write the schema, add tests, register the tool, update the tool inventory, add eval cases, and so on. Developers use Claude Code, and the project's CLAUDE.md is already long. The procedure is needed only a few times a month. Where should the architect put this guidance so that Claude Code applies it when relevant without bloating every session?

options.text: Append the full nine-step procedure to the project CLAUDE.md under a clear heading, so it is always in context and Claude Code can never miss it when a developer asks to add a new tool.
Package it as a project skill in .claude/skills/ with a clear description, so Claude Code loads the full steps only when a developer adds a tool or invokes the skill by name.
Keep the procedure on the team wiki and add a sentence to CLAUDE.md telling Claude Code to search the internet for the team's wiki page whenever it is asked to add a new tool.
Put it in each developer's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file, so it loads for them in every project and does not add to the size of the shared project file in the repository.

questions.explanation: Claude Code's docs draw the line directly: create a skill when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact, because a skill's body loads only when it is used, while CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session. Project skills live in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md and are committed so the whole team gets them. Only the skill's description sits in context by default; the nine steps load when the skill is invoked, by the developer or by Claude when the task calls for it.

whyWrong.A: Adding rarely used procedures to CLAUDE.md costs context in every session and reduces adherence to the rest of the file.
whyWrong.C: A sentence telling Claude to go and find a wiki page isn't reliable loading, and an internal wiki usually isn't reachable from the internet anyway.
whyWrong.D: User-level files aren't shared through source control, so teammates and new hires never receive the guidance. It also loads into unrelated projects.

questions.mindset: Put always-needed facts in CLAUDE.md and on-demand procedures in skills.

questions.stem: A fintech team's implementation guide states: "Never read or modify the .env files or anything under secrets/." The rule is in the project CLAUDE.md, yet an audit found a Claude Code session that opened a secrets file while debugging. The security lead wants this rule to hold in every session while developers still understand why it exists. Which TWO actions should the architect take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rewrite the CLAUDE.md rule in capital letters with words like CRITICAL and NEVER, and repeat it at both the top and the bottom of the file so it carries more weight with the model.
Add a step to the guide asking developers to review each session's transcript at the end of the day and report any access to the secrets files to the security lead for follow-up.
Add permission deny rules (or a PreToolUse hook that blocks the call) for those paths in the committed project settings, so the client enforces the rule whatever Claude decides.
Move the rule from CLAUDE.md into a skill named protect-secrets, so that Claude Code loads it on demand whenever it is about to work with configuration or credential files.
Keep a short explanation in CLAUDE.md of why secrets are off-limits and where to get test credentials, so the documented guidance and the enforced control stay aligned.

questions.explanation: Claude Code's docs are explicit: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, and to block an action regardless of what Claude decides you use permission rules or a PreToolUse hook. A must-always rule therefore needs an enforced control in the shared project settings. The documentation still matters: a short explanation of why and what to do instead (where test credentials come from) helps developers and Claude work with the control instead of around it. Document the guidance, and enforce the critical part.

whyWrong.A: Louder wording is still guidance, not enforcement. It may change behavior a little, but it can't guarantee the rule holds.
whyWrong.B: After-the-fact transcript review detects violations late and depends on people remembering. It doesn't prevent the access.
whyWrong.D: A skill loads only when invoked or judged relevant, so it is even less certain to be applied than CLAUDE.md, and it still enforces nothing.

questions.mindset: Documentation guides; settings and hooks enforce. Use both for rules that must always hold.

questions.stem: A customer complained about a wrong answer from an insurance assistant last Tuesday. When the team investigated, nobody could say which system prompt version or which model was in use at that time, because prompts are edited in a shared admin screen and the model setting was changed twice that week. What should the architecture documentation and implementation guidance require going forward?

options.text: Keep prompts in version control with a register of prompt versions, exact model IDs and their eval scores, and log the prompt version and model ID with every request.
Take a weekly screenshot of the admin screen showing the prompt and model setting, and store the images in a dated shared folder so the team can look back at past configurations.
Ask the model to state its own version and the date of its instructions at the start of every reply, so the information appears in each conversation transcript.
Lock the admin screen so that only the lead architect can edit prompts or change the model, which means there is always one person who knows the current setup.

questions.explanation: To reproduce and diagnose a production issue you need to know exactly what ran. That means treating prompts as versioned artifacts in source control, keeping a register that ties each prompt version and exact model identifier to its eval results, and logging both with every request. Anthropic's model-deprecation guidance also shows why exact model IDs must be recorded: models are retired, and you need to know what to re-test.

whyWrong.B: Weekly screenshots miss changes made between captures (the model changed twice in one week) and can't be tied to individual requests.
whyWrong.C: The model's own statement about its version isn't a reliable record, and it pollutes customer-facing replies.
whyWrong.D: Restricting editing to one person creates a bottleneck and a single point of knowledge, but still leaves no reliable record.

questions.mindset: Version prompts like code and log exactly what ran with every request.

questions.stem: An architect must document a new retrieval-augmented assistant for an audience that includes the executive sponsor, a security reviewer, and the engineers who will build it. Last time, a single 60-page design document was produced, and the sponsor and security reviewer said they could not find what they needed. Which documentation approach BEST serves all three audiences?

options.text: Write three independent documents from scratch, one per audience, each maintained by a different person, so that every audience gets content written entirely in its own language and level of detail.
Produce the same 60-page document again but add a detailed table of contents and a full index, so each reader can search out the sections that matter most to their role.
Replace written documentation with a recorded walkthrough video of the new system, since a video is easier for non-technical stakeholders to follow than a long written document.
Write a one-page overview with a context diagram, data flow and key decisions, linking to focused sections on data handling for the security review and implementation detail for engineers.

questions.explanation: Layered documentation gives every reader a shared entry point (purpose, context diagram, data flow from input to output, the pattern chosen and why), then links to the depth each role needs: data flow and controls for security, conventions and components for engineers. Because the layers share one source, they don't drift apart. This matches the general practice of an architecture overview that everyone reads plus focused supporting documents.

whyWrong.A: Three independently maintained documents will drift and start to contradict each other, which is worse than one hard-to-read document.
whyWrong.B: A table of contents doesn't fix the core problem: the sponsor still has no short summary and must hunt through engineering detail.
whyWrong.C: A video can't be searched, reviewed line by line or kept up to date easily, and a security review needs written, checkable detail.

questions.mindset: Layer documentation: one shared overview, with linked depth for each audience.

questions.stem: A hospital is rolling out a discharge-summary drafting assistant to nurses, most of whom are not technical. The architecture and runbooks are complete, but early pilot users either over-trusted drafts or refused to use the tool at all. What implementation guidance for end users will MOST help them use it safely and effectively?

options.text: Distribute the full architecture document to all nurses, so they understand how retrieval, prompts and the model work together and can judge each output from first principles.
Add a banner to every draft saying 'AI-generated content may contain errors', and otherwise leave nurses to develop their own ways of working with the tool over time.
Give a short quick-reference guide: what the tool does and does not do, what to check in every draft, when to escalate, and how to report a problem, with worked examples.
Run a one-time launch webinar on the benefits of generative AI in healthcare, and record it so that new staff, including future hires, can watch it as part of their standard onboarding.

questions.explanation: End users need practical guidance at their level: the intended and out-of-scope uses, the specific things to verify before signing off (the known limitations), what to do when something looks wrong, and how to report it so it feeds the improvement loop. Worked examples make the boundaries concrete. This calibrates trust in both directions, reducing blind acceptance and unwarranted rejection.

whyWrong.A: Architecture detail is the wrong level for nurses. It doesn't tell them what to check or when to escalate.
whyWrong.B: A generic disclaimer gives no guidance on what to check, so it neither prevents over-trust nor helps reluctant users.
whyWrong.D: A general benefits talk doesn't explain this tool's limits or the checks nurses must make, and it tends to raise expectations.

questions.mindset: Guide end users with the limits, checks and escalation path for their task, not the internals.

questions.stem: An architect's implementation guide tells teams to "use prompt caching" for a support assistant whose system prompt holds a large, stable policy section. In production, cost is far above the design estimate. Request logs show cache_read_input_tokens near zero on most calls: each team's code prepends a timestamp and the customer's account ID at the top of the system prompt and puts cache_control on the final block. Which addition to the implementation guide will MOST directly fix this?

options.text: Tell teams to add more cache_control breakpoints throughout the prompt, up to the maximum allowed, so that at least one section of every request matches a cached entry regardless of ordering.
Specify the prompt layout: tools and the stable policy section first, the cache breakpoint at the end of that stable content, per-request data after it, and verify cache reads are non-zero.
Tell teams to switch every breakpoint to the one-hour cache lifetime, so that cached entries survive long enough to be reused across many different customers' conversations throughout the whole day.

Add an instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to reuse its earlier reading of the stable policy section rather than processing it again, so that repeated requests cost fewer billed input tokens.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching matches on an exact prefix in the order tools, then system, then messages, and a change anywhere in that prefix invalidates everything after it. A timestamp or account ID at the top of the system prompt means no two requests share a prefix, so cache_read_input_tokens stays near zero wherever the breakpoint sits. The docs therefore say to place static content first and put cache_control on the last block whose prefix is identical across the requests you want to share a cache. The guide must prescribe that structure, not just the intent, and give teams a measurable check (usage.cache_read_input_tokens greater than zero on repeat calls) so they can see caching working.

whyWrong.A: Extra breakpoints cannot rescue a prefix that differs from the first token. The cache is hierarchical, so a change at the start invalidates every later section no matter how many breakpoints follow it.
whyWrong.C: Lifetime is irrelevant when nothing ever matches. A longer TTL only costs more on cache writes while reads stay at zero, because the per-request data still sits in front of the breakpoint.
whyWrong.D: Caching is server-side infrastructure keyed on the request prefix, not model behavior. Asking Claude to 'reuse its earlier reading' changes nothing about which tokens are processed or billed.

questions.mindset: Implementation guidance must prescribe the structure that makes the platform feature work, plus a way to verify it.

questions.stem: Five product teams are each building their own Claude-based summarization feature from the architect's written implementation guide. A review finds that each team has handled retries, logging, prompt storage and evaluation differently, and two teams shipped without running any evals. The architect wants future teams to implement the pattern consistently with minimal ongoing hand-holding. Which TWO additions will MOST improve consistency? Choose TWO.

options.text: A maintained reference implementation (template repository) showing retries with backoff, request logging, versioned prompts and an eval harness, which new teams start from.
A longer version of the written guide that describes each concern in more detail, with additional paragraphs on retries with backoff, request logging and evaluation best practice.
A definition of done that requires passing the agreed eval suite in CI before release, so a summarization feature cannot ship without measured quality against its agreed thresholds.
A rule that every team must use the largest available model, so that differences in output quality between the teams' implementations are minimized from the very start.
A central architecture team that writes every team's prompts and code on their behalf, so that the implementation is identical across all products by construction rather than by review.

questions.explanation: Prose guidance leaves every team to reinvent the details, which is how five different implementations appeared. A maintained reference implementation makes the right way the easy default: teams start with retries, logging, versioned prompts and an eval harness already in place. A definition of done enforced in CI (the eval suite must pass against agreed thresholds) turns the most important guidance into a gate, so no team can ship unmeasured. Anthropic's eval guidance treats evals as the way to measure and protect quality across changes.

whyWrong.B: More prose is still optional reading. The teams already had a written guide and diverged anyway.
whyWrong.D: Model choice doesn't make retries, logging or evaluation consistent, and it raises cost without regard to each task's needs.
whyWrong.E: Centralizing all the work creates a bottleneck and doesn't scale; the goal is for teams to build consistently on their own.

questions.mindset: Make the right way the default (templates) and gate the critical parts (evals in CI).
